title: Wash, and be clean (2 Kings 5:1–14)
hook: the general wanted something grand, and was told to wash in the Jordan

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Shunammite made room for a stranger and asked nothing back: I dwell among my people. Today, someone pulls up at Elisha's door with horses and chariots.

Horses, chariots, servants, and gifts of silver, gold and fine clothing. Naaman, captain of the army of the king of Aram, has come a long way, and he has come in style. The text calls him a great man, honored by his king, a mighty man of valor. And then a short phrase undoes all of it: he was a leper. He has a skin disease no rank can cure. Someone has told him there's a prophet in Israel who could heal him. So the whole procession stops at Elisha's door. And Elisha doesn't come out.
screen: `HORSES, CHARIOTS, SILVER, GOLD.` → `A GREAT MAN, BUT A LEPER.` → `ELISHA DOESN'T COME OUT.`

segments.voice: Instead, Elisha sends a messenger: go and wash in the Jordan seven times, and your flesh will be restored, and you will be clean. No ceremony. No prophet at the door. Naaman is furious, and the text lets us hear why. I thought he would surely come out to me, stand there, call on the name of his God, wave his hand over the spot, and heal me. He had pictured the whole scene in advance. Then the insult of the river itself: are not Abana and Pharpar, the rivers of Damascus, better than all the waters of Israel? Couldn't I wash in them and be clean? He turns and leaves in a rage. What stops him is not the prophet. It's his own servants. They call him, my father. If the prophet had asked you to do some great thing, wouldn't you have done it? "How much rather then, when he saith to thee, Wash, and be clean?" A sharp, kind question. Naaman was ready for a quest, a price, a drama worthy of a general. What he couldn't accept was something ordinary: a plain river, seven dips, no prophet at the bank. And yet he goes down to the Jordan, dips himself seven times, just as the man of God said, and his flesh comes back like the flesh of a little child, and he is clean. The cure was there from the first message. What stood in the way was Naaman's picture of how it should happen. The hard part wasn't the washing. It was getting down off the chariot.
screen: `GO AND WASH IN THE JORDAN.` · `I THOUGHT HE WOULD COME OUT.` · then, large: `WASH, AND BE CLEAN.` · then: `LIKE THE FLESH OF A LITTLE CHILD.`

segments.voice: Name something you've been stuck on, waiting for a big solution: a tense relationship, a messy room, a project you can't start. Ask what Naaman's servants asked: if the answer were something grand, would I do it, and what's the plain, ordinary step I keep stepping over? Name it to yourself, and in your mind, step down off the chariot.
Wash. The plain instruction a great general almost refused: go down into an ordinary river and dip, as the prophet said. Today's word.
Your line: getting down off the chariot. Sometimes the ordinary is the whole instruction. Day seven hundred seventy-three, done.

howItsDone: Jews read Naaman's healing as part of the book of Kings and as a haftarah alongside the Torah's laws of skin disease, which are read in the book of Leviticus.

chat.says: Why was Naaman so angry when Elisha told him to wash in the Jordan?
options: He expected a grand healing; a plain river and seven dips felt beneath him.
The Jordan was poisoned in those days, and he feared for his life.
He wanted to wash only once, and seven times seemed like a trick.
chat.meaning: Naaman thought Elisha would come out and wave his hand. His servants asked: if it were some great thing, wouldn't you have done it?

Naaman.meaning: captain of the army of Aram, a leper

Aram.meaning: a kingdom north of Israel, with Damascus its city

Jordan.meaning: the river where Naaman was told to wash
